fields.value: In one of three dialogue segments, the proposed role-based head-and-eye model was rated significantly more natural than the other models (p ≤ .05); no significant differences were found in the other two segments.

quotes.text: Since there were no significant differences between the four conditions in two of the three dialogue segments, we report the results of one of the dialogue segment in which a significant difference was found.

It was found that the proposed model ("PR H+E" model) which includes the role-based gaze control, and eyeball-accounted gaze aversion model, is evaluated to be significantly more natural than the other models (p-value ≤.05).

fields.value: The paper frames gaze as a nonverbal behavior that supports dialogue, including feedback, emotional communication, and regulation of dialogue flow; it studies role-based gaze and gaze aversion for multiparty dialogue.

quotes.text: Eye gaze conveys several functions in facilitating dialogue such as: to provide feedback, communicate emotional information, and regulate dialogue flow.

Thus, in order to improve the humanlikeness of gaze behaviors in humanoid robots, we consider the dialogue roles of participants in multi-party conversations, and the eyeball movements during gaze aversion, in this study.

fields.value: The paper describes gaze aversion as looking away from a dialogue participant’s face; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze-based attention.

quotes.text: In order to generate humanlike gazing in dialogue robots, gaze aversions (i.e., when looking away from the dialogue participant’s face) have also been considered in a few studies [15].

fields.value: Gaze helps regulate dialogue flow and is related to turn-taking and participants’ dialogue roles, including speaker, main listener/addressee, and sub-listener. Gaze aversion is considered in relation to humanlike gaze behavior.

fields.value: The proposed model combining role-based gaze control and eyeball-accounted gaze aversion was judged significantly more natural than the other tested models in one segment. The study did not isolate the contributions of role-based control and gaze aversion.

fields.value: The authors analyzed annotated three-party dialogue gaze patterns and implemented four gaze models: same-proportion head-only, same-proportion head-and-eye, proposed role-based head-and-eye, and proposed role-based head-only. Robot head and eye movements were generated from the role and gaze-aversion analyses; lips and head motions also used speech-driven methods.

quotes.text: For this study, the gaze directions (gaze targets), eyeball directions (pupil positions), holder of speaking floor and turn-taking points were manually labeled.
This is the proposed model that implements the gaze control and the gaze aversion systems based on the roles described in Section 3.
The lips and head motions were automatically generated from the speech signal based on the methods proposed in [8], [10].

fields.value: CommU, a humanoid robot with actuators to control head and eyeball movements, including eyeball pitch and yaw.

quotes.text: We then evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed gaze control model through subjective evaluations in a humanoid robot, CommU, which has actuators to control both head and eyeball movements.
Video clips were recorded for the motions generated in the robot, for each of the four models.
Gaze behaviors were generated in a humanoid robot, CommU, which allows eyeball control for both pitch and yaw directions.

fields.value: The robot’s ability to move its eyeballs enabled comparison of head-only with head-and-eye models; the authors report that the combined role-based and eyeball-accounted model appeared more natural, but they could not determine which component caused the effect.

quotes.text: To investigate the effects of eyeball movements, we implemented the same model as the baseline one, by adding eyeball movements along with the head movements.

However, in this experiment, we were not able to clarify which of the two factors, gaze aversion or role-based gaze control, had a stronger effect on the robot’s behavior, or whether the robot’s behavior became natural only when both factors were combined.

fields.value: The authors analyzed gaze and gaze aversion in three-person human conversations, then used those patterns to build role-based gaze models for the humanoid robot CommU. In video ratings, the model combining role-based gaze with eye movement during gaze aversion was judged more natural than the other models in one of three dialogue segments.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper describes gaze functions and role-based patterns in multiparty dialogue, evaluates naturalness effects, and details gaze-control models and the CommU embodiment. Its comparison of head-only and head-and-eye models also addresses how the robot’s eye movement capability shaped the study.
